name: Audience Adaptation Conventions
description: This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing audience adaptation code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing audience adaptation style guide.
content:
This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing audience adaptation code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing audience adaptation style guide.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Document any non-obvious audience adaptation decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
2. When multiple audience adaptation strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
3. Keep audience adaptation changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
4. Check that audience adaptation terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
5. Prefer explicit, readable audience adaptation solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
6. Validate audience adaptation outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
7. Keep audience adaptation outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
8. Measure before optimizing any audience adaptation bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
9. Re-check edge cases relevant to audience adaptation (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting audience adaptation assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not silently drop audience adaptation edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid introducing new audience adaptation abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for audience adaptation, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
